title: How the web works: one request's journey

questions.prompt: In which order do these happen when you open an HTTPS page?
options: TLS → DNS → TCP → HTTP request → app → database → response
DNS → TCP → HTTP request → TLS → app → database → response
DNS → TCP → TLS → HTTP request → database → app → response
DNS → TCP → TLS → HTTP request → app → database → response
questions.why: First an address (DNS), then a connection (TCP), then trust (TLS), then the request goes to the app, which asks the database.

wrong.0: TLS needs a connection, and a connection needs an address from DNS.
wrong.1: On HTTPS the request is sent inside TLS, so TLS comes first.
wrong.2: The browser never talks to the database. The app does.

questions.prompt: `curl: (6) Could not resolve host`. Which hop failed?
questions.why: Resolving means turning the name into an address. That is DNS.

wrong.0: No connection was tried yet, so TLS never started.
wrong.2: Without an address, the request never reached the app.
wrong.3: The database is two hops behind the app. Nothing got that far.

questions.prompt: The response is status 302 with `location: /login`. What happens next?
options: The browser makes a new request to /login
The page is shown, then replaced
questions.why: 3xx means "go elsewhere". The browser follows `location` with a new request.

wrong.1: A 302 usually has no page to show. The browser goes straight on.
wrong.3: A server that is down sends no status at all.

questions.prompt: The hosting edge answers 502. What does that mean?
options: The edge was reached, but it got no valid answer from the app behind it
questions.why: 502 Bad Gateway: the edge works; the hop behind it did not answer properly.

wrong.0: The edge answered, so DNS, TCP and TLS all worked.
wrong.1: That would be 401, from the app.

questions.prompt: Someone on the same Wi-Fi watches your HTTPS traffic. What can they NOT read?
options: The path, the headers and the body
Anything at all, including which site you visit
Everything; HTTPS only proves who the server is
questions.why: TLS encrypts the whole HTTP conversation. The host name is still visible in DNS and in TLS.

wrong.1: The host name is visible: DNS asks for it, and TLS names it.
wrong.2: TLS encrypts all of the request, not one field.
wrong.3: TLS also encrypts. Proving identity is only half of it.

questions.prompt: You changed a page. The browser shows the old one; `curl` shows the new one. Which cache is most likely?
questions.why: `curl` keeps no copy. Only the browser kept the old page.

wrong.0: Both would go to the same server, so both would see the same page.
wrong.2: TLS keeps no copy of pages.

questions.prompt: An evidence file contains a full `set-cookie` session value. What is wrong?
options: A live session was written down; it must be removed
Nothing, because the file is in docs/
questions.why: Whoever has a session cookie is signed in as you, without a password.

wrong.0: A session cookie is as good as a password while it is valid.
wrong.2: A folder name protects nothing. docs/ is often committed and shared.
wrong.3: A session cookie gives the same access as a password.

questions.prompt: GPIS: why must a page with a student's scores never be stored in a shared edge cache?
options: The next visitor could be given another person's page
questions.why: A shared cache gives the same stored copy to everyone who asks for that address.

wrong.0: A cache makes pages faster, not slower.
wrong.1: Edge caches store HTML all the time.
wrong.3: Scores change rarely. Privacy is the reason.
